Hochwohlgebohrner Herr, Insonders Hochzuehrender Herr Lieutenant! Schämen muß ich mir wohl, Ew. Hochwohlgebl. gütiges Schreiben so lange danckbahrlich unbeantwortet gelaßen zu haben, rechnete ich nicht an ihr gütiges Entschuldigen, so würde es jezt nicht von neuen Wagen Dieselben mit meinen gegenwärtigen zu belästigen.

daß ich Schleßen und Brau verlassen müßen, worinnen beinahe 49 Jahre meist glücklich und froh gelebt, und bei in zu meinen Auffenthalt gewählt, um meine dringünste Geschäfte der Verlust meines Vermögens, hier beßer zu betreiben wenn möglich noch etwas zu retten, wäiIhnen vielleicht nicht gantz unberauß sein Allein noch sind hierzu die Außachten nicht sehr klar, und selbst mein alte gewesener Sachwalter in Josen Hl. Weltzer, der sich jezt auch hier aufhält, der die Polnische Justitz zu können glaubt, hat wenig Hoffnung, das Ausweitige Departement hat sich für mich an den Dresden Huffe verraut, allen auch dieser, will zwar daß die vorher bezahlten

Schulden nachgesucht werden könten, waß aber die Güter selbst betrift, so sucht Er - absehen kein officieller Befehl des Keisers hiezu vorhanden. die damaligen Polnischen Richter zu entschuldigen und die tilsitum friedens articulae so für und hierinnen sein, nicht darauf anwendbahr zu machen.

Der hiesige Franzosische Gesante, bei dem voriges sehr bei meinen Hiersein war, macht mir in der Art hoffnung: daß wenn kein ausdrückliche Keiserliches Befehl hierzu vorhanden, und ich die official Ihm geben könnte, Er sich meine vor, nehmen wolte. Endlich habe ich den selbst vom Sächsischen Hofe, welcher sagt, daß die von Dąbska in desden den Keiser und die zurückgabe der Güter gebeten — So keiselich Majestät bloß der damaligen Pluischen Regierung Ihre Bittschrift zugeschickten Hirauf haben Die Pluische Commissarien befohlen der am Dąbska die Güter wieder zugeben. Gegenwärtig bin beschäftigt dieses Übersehen gelaßen, und werde sehen in wie weit

der Französische hiesige Gesente, sich dieser Sachen annehmen wird, weide auch nicht verfohlen Fr. Hochwohlgebl. so gleich davon Nachricht gegeben, damit Fr. Hochfürstlich Durchlaucht die ich mich zu Gnaden zu empfehlen bitte davon gleichfals villeicht gebrauch machen könten.

Wie werde die Wohltaten vergeßen so ich durch diesen Fürsten erhilt, meine Anhänglichkeit kann und wird nie sterben.

Ist denn noch keine Sententz aus den ersten Tribunal über des Fürsten Trombſchyner Güter heraus? Hütten Ew. Hochwohlgeb. wohl die Güte mir wißen zu laßen, 1) wenns möglich abschriftlich - waß die Friedens Ruhte feurteilt, und 2t waß die Sententz mit den triebonal besagt hat?

Neues wolle Ihnen gerne mit fielen allein auß in einem Tage hier für gewis ausgegeben. wird den andern bezweiffelt, und den dritten verdrängt eine zweite oft wiedersprechend

die erſten So viel scheint aber doch aus allen hervorzuleuchten, daß man einen baldigen Ausbruch des Krieger in Norden vermutet. Würde es im Abend klar so würde es in Norden brennen sei ist glaube ich der Ableiter. zu Erwaltung einer zütigen Antwort und Verzeihung meiner Nachläßigkeit verharre in der vollkommensten Hochachtung lebenslang Ew Hochwohlgebohren

Michalina z Prusimskich Dąbska, later Miączyńska

mentions_english.display: Michalina z Prusimskich Dąbska, later Miączyńska

translation.en:
Right Honourable Sir, Most particularly Highly Honoured Lieutenant! I must indeed be ashamed to have left Your Right Honourable's kind letter so long unanswered with my thanks; did I not count upon your kind indulgence, I should not now venture anew to burden you with the present one.

That I have had to leave [uncertain: Silesia] and [uncertain: Brau], wherein I lived near 49 years mostly happy and content, and chose [illegible] for my residence, in order the better to pursue here my most pressing affairs, the loss of my fortune, and if possible still to salvage something, will perhaps not be entirely unknown to you. Only, the prospects in this matter are not yet very clear, and even my old former counsel in [uncertain: Josen], Mr Weltzer, who is now likewise staying here, and who believes he knows the Polish justice, has little hope; the Foreign Department has [uncertain: pledged] itself on my behalf to the [uncertain: Dresden Huffe], but this one too would have it that the previously paid

debts might be recovered; but as concerns the estates themselves, he seeks — setting aside that no official command of the Emperor exists for this — to excuse the then Polish judges and to render the peace articles of Tilsit, so far as they are in favour of and herein, not applicable to the case.

The French envoy here, with whom [uncertain: formerly] there was much during my stay here, gives me hope in this manner: that if no express Imperial command exists for it, and I could give him the official [document], he would take my [cause] upon himself. At length I have it from the Saxon court itself, which says that the lady Dąbska in Dresden petitioned the Emperor for the restitution of the estates — that His Imperial Majesty merely forwarded her petition to the then [uncertain: Prussian] government. Upon this the [uncertain: Prussian] commissioners ordered that the estates be given back to the lady Dąbska. At present I am occupied in having this [uncertain: transcribed], and shall see how far

the French envoy here will take up these matters, and I have also not failed to give Your Right Honourable notice of it at once, so that His Most Serene Highness — to whose grace I beg to be commended — might perhaps likewise make use of it.

I shall never forget the benefactions I received through this Prince; my attachment can and will never die.

Is there then still no sentence out of the first tribunal concerning the Prince's Trąbczyn estates? Would Your Right Honourable have the goodness to let me know, 1) if possible in copy — what the peace [uncertain: rod] adjudged, and 2nd, what the sentence with the tribunal has declared?

News I would gladly [give] you in plenty, only what is here given out for certain on one day is doubted on the next, and on the third a second, often contradictory, one displaces

the first. This much, however, does seem to shine forth from it all, that an early outbreak of war in the north is surmised. Were it clear in the evening, then it would be burning in the north — that, I believe, is the conductor. Awaiting a kindly answer and the pardon of my negligence, I remain in the most perfect esteem, lifelong, Your Right Honourable's

Berlin

the 15th of August 1811

Stalauer Street:

No. 13 wholly obedient and faithful [uncertain: Euder] servant, von Sanitz

text_english:
Right Honourable Sir, Most particularly Highly Honoured Lieutenant! I must indeed be ashamed to have left Your Right Honourable's kind letter so long unanswered with my thanks; did I not count upon your kind indulgence, I should not now venture anew to burden you with the present one.

That I have had to leave [uncertain: Silesia] and [uncertain: Brau], wherein I lived near 49 years mostly happy and content, and chose [illegible] for my residence, in order the better to pursue here my most pressing affairs, the loss of my fortune, and if possible still to salvage something, will perhaps not be entirely unknown to you. Only, the prospects in this matter are not yet very clear, and even my old former counsel in [uncertain: Josen], Mr Weltzer, who is now likewise staying here, and who believes he knows the Polish justice, has little hope; the Foreign Department has [uncertain: pledged] itself on my behalf to the [uncertain: Dresden Huffe], but this one too would have it that the previously paid

debts might be recovered; but as concerns the estates themselves, he seeks — setting aside that no official command of the Emperor exists for this — to excuse the then Polish judges and to render the peace articles of Tilsit, so far as they are in favour of and herein, not applicable to the case.

The French envoy here, with whom [uncertain: formerly] there was much during my stay here, gives me hope in this manner: that if no express Imperial command exists for it, and I could give him the official [document], he would take my [cause] upon himself. At length I have it from the Saxon court itself, which says that the lady Dąbska in Dresden petitioned the Emperor for the restitution of the estates — that His Imperial Majesty merely forwarded her petition to the then [uncertain: Prussian] government. Upon this the [uncertain: Prussian] commissioners ordered that the estates be given back to the lady Dąbska. At present I am occupied in having this [uncertain: transcribed], and shall see how far

the French envoy here will take up these matters, and I have also not failed to give Your Right Honourable notice of it at once, so that His Most Serene Highness — to whose grace I beg to be commended — might perhaps likewise make use of it.

I shall never forget the benefactions I received through this Prince; my attachment can and will never die.

Is there then still no sentence out of the first tribunal concerning the Prince's Trąbczyn estates? Would Your Right Honourable have the goodness to let me know, 1) if possible in copy — what the peace [uncertain: rod] adjudged, and 2nd, what the sentence with the tribunal has declared?

News I would gladly [give] you in plenty, only what is here given out for certain on one day is doubted on the next, and on the third a second, often contradictory, one displaces

the first. This much, however, does seem to shine forth from it all, that an early outbreak of war in the north is surmised. Were it clear in the evening, then it would be burning in the north — that, I believe, is the conductor. Awaiting a kindly answer and the pardon of my negligence, I remain in the most perfect esteem, lifelong, Your Right Honourable's

Berlin

the 15th of August 1811

Stalauer Street:

No. 13 wholly obedient and faithful [uncertain: Euder] servant, von Sanitz
summary_en: Sanitz explains his removal from Silesia and Brau after nearly 49 years to pursue the loss of his fortune and the recovery of estates taken by the Dąbska woman; his former legal agent Weltzer in Josen holds out little hope of Polish justice, the Dresden court excuses the Polish judges and denies the Peace of Tilsit's application, while the French envoy may take up his cause if Imperial orders are lacking. He asks for copies of the judgment and tribunal sentence in the Prince's Trombschyner suit, and reports rumours of imminent war in the North.
summary_de: Sanitz berichtet von seiner Übersiedlung nach Berlin, um den Verlust seines Vermögens und die Rückforderung seiner an die Dąbska gefallenen Güter zu betreiben; sein früherer Justitiar Weltzer gibt wenig Hoffnung, das Departement der auswärtigen Angelegenheiten wandte sich an den Dresdner Hof, der die polnischen Richter entschuldigt und den Tilsiter Frieden für unanwendbar hält. Der französische Gesandte stellt Hilfe in Aussicht, falls kein kaiserlicher Befehl vorliegt. Bitte um Abschriften des Friedensspruchs und des Tribunalsurteils zu den fürstlichen Trombschyner Gütern; erwartet Kriegsausbruch im Norden.
